bibliography.abstract: The accessibility of medical facilities is directly related to the quality of residents’ lives and has attracted increasing attention from both researchers and policymakers. However, previous studies have paid little attention to urban–rural inequalities in the accessibility of tiered public hospitals in superlarge cities and fail to provide a comprehensive assessment that integrates both physician and bed resources. With Chongqing, China, as the study area, this study applied the Gaussian-based two-step floating catchment area (G2SFCA) method to measure the car-based potential accessibility of tiered public hospitals, with both physician and bed resources accounted for. The Dagum Gini coefficient was employed to decompose the urban–rural and regional inequalities in medical accessibility. The results show that, within each hospital grade, the average accessibility of the city proper of Chongqing is greater than that of other regions for both bed-based and physician-based measures. In contrast, the average accessibility of the Wuling Mountain Area in Southeast Chongqing exceeds that of the Three Gorges Reservoir Area in Northeast Chongqing only for Grade III hospitals (both bed-based and physician-based) and for bed-based accessibility of Grade II hospitals, when the regions are compared within the same hospital grade. Bed-based and physician-based accessibility are significantly positively correlated at the subdistrict/township level, with Pearson coefficients of 0.982, 0.913, and 0.620 for Grade III, Grade II, and Grade I/ungraded public hospitals, respectively, indicating a hierarchical gradient of increasing spatial consistency with the hospital level. The primary source of inequality varies by hospital grade and resource type. Urban–rural inequality is dominant for Grade II hospitals, whereas interregional inequality is more pronounced for physician-based accessibility in Grade III and Grade I/ungraded hospitals. This study concludes that, for each hospital grade in Chongqing’s public hospitals, the city proper of Chongqing exhibit higher average bed‑based and physician‑based accessibility. Spatial consistency between bed‑based and physician‑based accessibility declines for lower‑grade hospitals. Furthermore, the dominant source of accessibility inequality shifts between urban–rural and interregional dimensions, depending on hospital grade and resource type. This study challenges the conventional assumption that urban–rural inequality is universally the primary contradiction, demonstrating that healthcare inequality is a multidimensional phenomenon shaped jointly by facility hierarchy, the resource dimension, and spatial partitioning, thereby providing a more nuanced analytical framework for understanding spatial inequality in healthcare resources.
bibliography.title: Urban–Rural and Regional Inequalities in the Accessibility of Tiered Public Hospitals in Chongqing, China: A Comprehensive Assessment of Physician and Bed Resources

en.caveats: The accessibility measurements are based solely on car travel, which may not reflect the actual transit modes used by lower-income or rural populations.
en.what: This study measured car-based accessibility to tiered public hospitals in Chongqing, China, using the Gaussian-based two-step floating catchment area (G2SFCA) method to evaluate both physician and bed resources. Applying the Dagum Gini coefficient at the subdistrict and township level, the analysis revealed that the city proper maintains higher average accessibility than other regions across all hospital grades. It also identified a hierarchical gradient in spatial consistency, with Pearson correlation coefficients between bed and physician accessibility dropping from 0.982 for Grade III hospitals to 0.620 for Grade I/ungraded hospitals.
en.why: The findings challenge the common assumption that urban-rural disparities are always the primary driver of healthcare inequality, demonstrating instead that the dominant source of inequality shifts between urban-rural and interregional dimensions depending on the specific hospital grade and resource type.
